newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo accusations part of factional war - Radical.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo accusations part of factional war - Radical.

text.p: The leader of Argentina's opposition Radicals Tuesday said charges by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo that ministers covered up graft probes was just a clash between competing corrupt factions.

"We are witnessing a rupture between mafias, not an accusation against the mafia," said the Radical Party's Rodolfo Terragno, quoted by the private DyN news agency, using the word "mafia" loosely to refer to corruption rings.
He said Cavallo was "equally responsible" for government corruption with members of the government such as Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan.
Cavallo told local radio earlier Tuesday that Corach and Jassan were manipulating judges and trying to cover up corruption probes.
A leading figure of the center-left Frepaso alliance, Senator Graciela Fernandez Meijide, also saw Cavallo's attacks on his former colleagues as more of a feud than an assault on corruption.

"You could almost say or suspect that one sector wants everything for itself, that what it wants is to wipe the other sector out. But not corruption, because corruption is everywhere and always linked to power," she said.

Cavallo's accusations came a week after President Carlos Menem announced a "crusade" against corruption and launched a major probe into a $3 billion smuggling ring within the nation's customs service.

Another disaffected one-time Menem employee, former Interior Minister Gustavo Beliz, also added his volley to the barrage of accusations, saying Monday that Argentines did not believe the president was sincere in fighting graft.
Former Radical President Raul Alfonsin said Beliz's accusations were of the gravest nature: "Nothing of the sort has ever been heard of a president of the nation."
Menem sacked Cavallo in July, ending their often stormy partnership amid public outcry against austerity measures and a pay rise for Economy Ministry officials.
The former minister, considered the architect of Argentina's economic reforms, announced last week he was returning to politics to combat corruption.
